beats.caption: An ATM program lets a company sell new shares bit by bit into the market
beats.text: Instead of one big marketed deal, the company files a shelf registration with the SEC and signs a sales agreement with one or more brokers. The board sets a dollar cap, say $1-2 billion, and nothing has to be sold on any given day.

beats.caption: The broker drips shares into normal trading at the market price
beats.text: On days the company chooses, the broker sells newly issued shares into ordinary trading, often a small slice of daily volume so the price is not knocked down. There is no roadshow and no fixed discount; the broker takes a commission of around 1-3%.

beats.caption: Cash comes back over weeks or months until the cap is used
beats.text: Proceeds land in the company's account as trades settle. The company reports how much it sold, and at what average price, in its quarterly filings or a prospectus supplement. It can pause when the stock is weak and sell faster when it is strong.

beats.caption: Every share sold grows the share count and dilutes existing holders
beats.text: New shares are new claims on the same business. If a company with 500 million shares sells 25 million, each old holder owns about 5% less of it. The trade is worth it only if the cash earns more than the ownership given up.

beats.caption: Cash-hungry growth companies lean on it; traders watch it as steady supply
beats.text: AI infrastructure builders that need capital fast use ATMs alongside debt. A large open program is a steady seller in the market, which can cap rallies, so traders watch filings for new or upsized ATMs. Related: CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS), Super Micro Computer (SMCI), Applied Digital (APLD).
